claims.text: For US-sponsored roles the Infosys group filed 1,900 Labor Condition Applications in FY2025 with a median committed base wage of $92,581 (p25 $85,925, p75 $110,157) — but these describe US worksites and say nothing directly about an Indian offer.
Those filings sweep in four related employers (Infosys Limited, Infosys BPM, Infosys Public Services and Infosys McCamish Systems), so the median is a group figure rather than one entity's pay band.

The 20-F states that compensation increases may be delayed in adverse market conditions while competitors still raise, and names that as a driver of attrition — pay policy here is explicitly cyclical.

gaps.reason: no free structured compensation source exists for the Indian market: AmbitionBox is Naukri-owned and scrape-hostile, and Indian postings rarely publish ranges. No estimate is offered here because any number would be invented.
gaps.suggested_fallback: search AmbitionBox and Levels.fyi for 'Infosys Technology Lead Bengaluru', treat what you find as dated anecdote, and compare the offer against your own current package rather than a market median

claims.text: The public GitHub organisation has 102 repositories and the recently active ones are digital-public-infrastructure components (esignet, inji-certify, mimoto), committed to within the last two days — real engineering, but almost none of it carries external stars or contributors.

The loudest public engineering discussion of this company remains a 2022 credential-leak thread; there is little recent first-hand engineering commentary either way, which for a 328,000-person company means the public record is close to silent.

The company describes AI adoption as a strategic risk in its own filing ('Our investments in or use of AI technologies may not be successful'), which is a more candid framing than the marketing site offers.

gaps.reason: no dated first-hand employee accounts from the last 18 months were found, so wlb_sentiment is unset; at this headcount, absence of public commentary is not evidence either way
gaps.suggested_fallback: ask to speak to two engineers on the specific delivery account, and ask what the on-call and client-hours expectations are for that account rather than for the company

claims.text: Revenue grew from $12.78bn (FY2020) to $19.28bn (FY2025), an 8.6% compound rate, but only 3.9% in the most recent year — the growth curve has flattened, not reversed.
Operating income rose to $4.07bn while net income was flat at $3.16bn: margins are being defended even as growth slows.

Cash and equivalents nearly doubled to $2.86bn over two years, and the exchange reports return on equity of 36.7% with an operating margin of 27.1% — this is a cash-generative business, not one under funding pressure.
R&D spend is $153m against $19.3bn of revenue (0.8%), which is characteristic of a services business: the money follows billable delivery, not product engineering.

The 20-F risk factors put client concentration and fixed-price delivery first: 'Our failure to complete fixed-price and fixed-timeframe contracts within budget and on time may negatively affect our profitability', and 'Our client contracts are often conditional upon our performance'.
Headcount was 328,594 at 31 March 2026 against 323,578 a year earlier: growth of 1.5%, far below the revenue growth rate, which is what a services company doing more with the same people looks like.

310,887 of those 328,594 employees are service-delivery professionals, so the ratio of delivery to everything else is roughly 19 to 1 — worth knowing before assuming a platform-engineering career path.
A management change was disclosed to the exchange on 24 August 2026 under Regulation 30; senior churn immediately before an offer decision is worth asking about.

claims.text: The company itself flags volatility in Indian attrition as an ongoing risk, tying it to wage increases, share price movement and competitor hiring — the closest thing to an audited satisfaction number that exists here.
The 20-F also names hybrid-work friction directly: employee preference for remote working set against client expectations of return-to-office is listed as a risk to attrition and client satisfaction.

gaps.suggested_fallback: read the quarterly attrition percentage in the last four results releases (BSE announcements) — it is audited, dated and specific, unlike a rating; then search the rating sites yourself for colour

narrative.summary: Infosys is a financially solid, cash-generative services company whose growth has flattened to about 4% a year while margins hold near 27%. Headcount grew 1.5% against that, so the offer sits in a business doing more with roughly the same number of people. Compensation cannot be answered from any free structured source for the Indian market, and this dossier does not guess: the number to compare against is your current package, not a market median someone invented. The company's own filing is unusually candid about attrition, cyclical pay increases and return-to-office friction, and those are the three things worth pressing on before accepting.

strengths.text: Cash of $2.86bn, ROE of 36.7% and a 27% operating margin: no funding risk here
Margins are being defended as growth slows, rather than earnings falling with revenue
A deep US sponsorship record (1,900 LCA filings in FY2025) if a transfer is ever on the table

concerns.text: Revenue growth has fallen to 3.9%, well below the six-year 8.6% CAGR
R&D is 0.8% of revenue and 95% of staff are in service delivery — this is a delivery career, not a product one
The company names delayed wage increases and hybrid-work friction as attrition drivers in its own 20-F
Compensation for the Indian market is a genuine data gap, and a management change was filed three days before this dossier

questions_to_ask: Which client account is this role attached to, and how long does that contract run?
What was voluntary attrition on that account over the last four quarters?
Is the compensation revision cycle on schedule this year, and when was the last one?
What are the return-to-office and client-hours expectations for this specific engagement?
How does someone in this role move from delivery into platform or product work here?
